steps.t: By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Find a square number as the result of multiplying a number by itself. Show that square numbers can be built as square arrays. Explain the link between consecutive odd numbers and square numbers. Explain why a number is not a square number. Build a triangular number, and the next one from the one before.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Squares and roots A square number comes from multiplying a whole number by itself - 4 x 4 = 16, so 16 is a square number, and its square root is 4. Part 2 of 3 Cubes and cube roots A cube number comes from multiplying a whole number by itself three times - stack a square, three layers high, and you have a cube. Part 3 of 3 Triangular numbers A triangular number is built from rows that grow by one each time - 1, then 1+2, then 1+2+3 - and can be drawn as a triangle of dots.

Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them. Step 1 A square number makes a square Take a number, and lay out that many rows of that many dots. If you get a square, the total is a SQUARE NUMBER. 4 rows of 4 dots is 16, so 16 is a square number, and we write it 4², read "four squared". Slide the side of the square and watch the total. Dots along each side: 4 16 = 4² The first twelve square numbers The little 2 means "times itself". 4² is 4 × 4 = 16, not 4 × 2. Say it "four squared", because it is the number of dots in a four-by-four square. Every square number is a number multiplied by itself. Step 2 Growing squares: add the next odd number To turn a 3-by-3 square into a 4-by-4 square you add an L shape down one side and along the bottom. That is 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 new dots. Every L is an odd number, and each one is 2 bigger than the last. So the square numbers go 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and the gaps between them go 3, 5, 7, 9. Slide to grow the square and watch the L. Grow from 3 × 3 to 4 × 4 The sequence so far Odd numbers build squares. 1 + 3 = 4, then + 5 = 9, then + 7 = 16, then + 9 = 25. Add the first five odd numbers and you get 5². That is why the gaps between square numbers keep growing: this is a sequence, but NOT one with a "same step every time" rule. Spot the mistake Your teacher says: 3 + 5 + 7 must make a square number, because they are consecutive odd numbers. Step 3 Is it a square number? Given a number of dots, try to arrange them into a full square. If they fit exactly, it is a square number. If some are left over, it sits BETWEEN two square numbers. Pick a number and see the biggest square you can make. How many dots Working Know the squares up to 12² by heart and you can answer this without any dots. They are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36,

steps.h: Square roots: the question the other way round
steps.t: Step 1 asked "what is 7 squared?" and the answer was 49. A SQUARE ROOT asks the opposite: here are 49 dots, how many go along each side of the square? The answer is 7, and it is written √49 = 7. The dots below are in a heap. Pick the side you think will use every one of them, and watch what happens if you pick too few or too many. Find the square root of How many along each side? Working The roots worth knowing by heart Roots that are not whole numbers A root undoes a square. 7² = 49 and √49 = 7, so squaring a number and then taking the square root brings you back to where you started. That is why knowing the squares from Step 1 by heart gives you the roots for free: read the list backwards. And a number that is not a square number has a root that is not a whole number. The best you can say is which two whole numbers it lies between.

A square number is a square of dots. A CUBE number is a cube of blocks: 3 blocks long, 3 wide and 3 high is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 blocks. We write that 3³ and say "three cubed". The teal top is one layer, and one layer is a square number. The cube is that many layers deep, so a cube number is a square number stacked. Slide the edge and count the blocks. Blocks along each edge: 3 27 = 3³ Squares and cubes side by side The little 3 means three copies multiplied, not "times 3". 3³ is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Two wrong answers both land on 9. One stops at the square, 3 × 3. The other reads the little 3 as "add it three times", 3 + 3 + 3. Watch the two columns in the table pull apart. At an edge of 2 the cube is only 4 more than the square. By an edge of 6 it is 216 against the square's 36, six times as many. Adding one to the edge of a cube adds a whole new layer, plus a strip down two of its sides.

steps.h: Cube roots: how long is the edge?
steps.t: Step 4 undid a square, and this undoes a cube. Here is a pile of blocks. If they build a solid cube with none left over and no gaps, how many go along each edge? That number is the CUBE ROOT, written ∛64 = 4. Pick an edge and the cube gets built. You can see whether it swallows the pile exactly, runs out early, or asks for more than you have. Find the cube root of How many along each edge? Working The cube roots worth knowing Roots that are not whole numbers The same number has a different square root and cube root. √64 = 8, because 8 × 8 = 64. ∛64 = 4, because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. The square root splits the number into two equal parts multiplied; the cube root splits it into three. And there are far fewer cubes to recognise than squares. Up to 216 there are fourteen square numbers and only six cube numbers. So a cube root is usually found by trying two or three edges rather than remembered. Step 7 Triangular numbers: rows that grow by one Put 1 dot on the top row, 2 on the next, 3 on the next, and you build a triangle. The number of dots is a TRIANGULAR number: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Adding all those rows up is slow, so there is a trick. Turn a second triangle upside down, push it against the first, and the two make a neat rectangle. Slide the rows, then press the second view to see it happen. How many rows: 4 One triangle Two triangles make a rectangle 10 dots in 4 rows Every triangle, and what it makes with the one before Two triangles make a rectangle, and two triangles in a row make a square. A triangle of 4 rows and an upside-down copy fit into a 4 by 5 rectangle of 20 dots. So one triangle is 20 ÷ 2 = 10. That is where rows × (rows + 1) ÷ 2 comes from. It works however many rows you have, without adding a single one of them up. The other pairing is a surprise. Add two trian

steps.t: By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Identify missing numbers in linear sequences. Explain why a sequence is linear. Find the difference between terms in a sequence. Use a term-to-term rule to extend a sequence. Work out a recursion rule from terms that are not consecutive.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Sequences and rules A sequence follows a rule from one term to the next - a term-to-term rule tells you exactly how to get from any term to the one after it. Part 2 of 3 Linear sequences A linear sequence changes by the same amount every time - find that difference once, and you can extend the sequence as far as you like. Part 3 of 3 Patterns in shapes A growing pattern of shapes hides a number sequence - count the pieces in each shape, and the rule for the shapes is the rule for the numbers too.
Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them.

steps.h: Sequences with a rule: start, then keep doing it
steps.t: A sequence is a list of numbers in order, and a term is one number in the list. A rule like "start at 5 and add 4" makes the whole sequence: each term comes from the one before it. Pick a start number and a rule, then read the terms off the strip. The arrows show the rule being used again and again. Start at 3 5 10 50 100 1 The rule add 3 add 4 add 7 add 25 subtract 3 subtract 6 double add 0.5 How many terms: 6 Working Two things make a sequence: where it starts and the rule. "Add 4" starting at 5 gives 5, 9, 13, 17. The same rule starting at 3 gives 3, 7, 11, 15: different sequence, same rule. And the rule is used one time FEWER than the number of terms: to reach the 6th term you use it 5 times. Step 9 Find the rule from the terms Now the sequence is given and the rule is hidden. Look at the GAP between one term and the next. If the gap is the same every time, the rule is "add that" or "subtract that". If the gaps change, look closer: maybe each term is double the last, or maybe the gaps are the odd numbers from Step 2. Pick a sequence and reveal it one move at a time. Pick a sequence 1 · Show the gaps 2 · Say the rule 3 · Next two terms Working Check the rule on EVERY gap, not just the first. 2, 4, 6 looks like "add 2" and 2, 4, 8 looks like "add 2" for one gap. But the next gap is 4, so the rule there is "double". One gap can fool you; two or three gaps cannot.

steps.t: In the last two steps you knew the rule and worked out the terms. Now you know two facts and have to work out two numbers. A shape standing in for a number nobody has told you yet is where algebra begins. Two facts about two shapes are always exactly enough. One would leave you guessing and three could contradict each other. They add to … and differ by … 7 is the triangle All six, side by side Adding the two facts is the trick, and it works because one shape cancels itself out. Put ▲ + ● = 10 underneath ▲ − ● = 4 and add them. The ● is added once and taken away once, so it disappears entirely. That leaves ▲ + ▲ = 14. That is one shape on its own, and halving it finishes the job. Subtracting the facts instead makes the ▲ disappear the same way. Two facts, two unknowns. One fact on its own leaves a whole list of answers. "They add to 10" is true of 9 and 1, 8 and 2, 7 and 3 and more. The second fact is what cuts the list down to one. And the shapes are only placeholders. A letter would do exactly the same job, which is what secondary school does. Write x and y instead of ▲ and ● and nothing else about the method changes. Step 11 Squares and cubes hiding in a sequence Step 8 said to look at the gaps, and that if they are all the same the rule is "add that". So what do you do when the gaps are NOT the same? Look at the gaps of the gaps. Squares and cubes turn up as sequences all the time, and this is how you catch them. Pick a sequence and say what is hiding in it. Pick a sequence What is hiding in it? The same gap every time Square numbers Cube numbers The gaps, and the gaps of those Working The gaps of the gaps are the giveaway. Every square-number sequence settles on the same one: 2, every single time. That holds whether th

steps.h: Shape patterns: count, then find the rule
steps.t: Patterns made of matchsticks or dots grow by a rule too. Count how many pieces pattern 1, pattern 2 and pattern 3 use, write the counts as a sequence, and the gap tells you the rule. Then you can say how many pieces pattern 10 needs without building it. Pick a pattern and slide through it. Pick a pattern Pattern number: 3 Working The gap is what one more piece of the pattern costs. One more square on the end of a row of matchstick squares needs 3 sticks, not 4, because it shares a side. That is why the counts go up in 3s. Look at the picture to see WHY the rule is what it is, and the sequence to see WHAT it is.

steps.h: Steps on a number line: decimals, and below zero
steps.t: A rule does not have to be a whole number, and a sequence does not have to stop at zero. "Start at 2, subtract 0.5" gives 2, 1.5, 1, 0.5, 0, −0.5. Watch the hops on the line: every hop is the same size, and the line simply carries on past zero into the negative numbers. Pick a start and a step. Start at: 2 The step add 0.5 add 1.5 add 2 add 3 subtract 0.5 subtract 2 subtract 3 Working Going down past zero. 1, then 1 − 3 is −2, not 2. On the line, subtracting means hopping LEFT, and the numbers left of zero are negative: −1, −2, −3. The hops stay the same size, so the pattern does not change just because the sign did.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Use the order of operations correctly, where there are no brackets. Use related facts and inverse operations for missing number problems. Use a test of divisibility to recognise multiples of 4. Explain what a prime number is. Use the sieve of Eratosthenes to find prime numbers to 100.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Odd, even and the order of operations Whole numbers are either odd or even, and a calculation with more than one operation must be done in the correct order, or the answer changes. Part 2 of 3 Factors and multiples A factor divides exactly into a number; a multiple is what you get by multiplying it. Every number shares factors with some numbers and not others. Part 3 of 3 Divisibility and primes A divisibility rule lets you check whether a number divides exactly without doing the whole division. A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them.

steps.h: The odd numbers, and what they add up to
steps.t: The odd numbers are the simplest sequence of all: start at 1 and add 2 for ever. They are the numbers you cannot share into two equal piles, and on the strip below they are every other one. Two things are worth knowing about them, and neither needs counting. One is where any odd number sits in the list. The other is what happens when you add the first few of them up. How many odd numbers: 4 Added end to end 16 = 4² Working Where does an odd number sit? Halve the next number up. Every position, its odd number, and the running total Step 2 showed this from the other side. There, each L you added to a square was the next odd number, which is why the squares grew 1, 4, 9, 16. Here is the same fact read as a list: add up the first few odd numbers and you always land exactly on a square. The other half of this step is the position. Counting along to the 50th odd number is slow, but 2 × 50 − 1 = 99 is quick. Going back the other way, (99 + 1) ÷ 2 = 50 tells you where 99 sits without counting a single one.
steps.g: addition division fraction geometry odd and even position

steps.h: The even numbers, and the rectangle they make
steps.t: The even numbers are the other half of the strip: start at 2 and add 2 for ever. They are the numbers you CAN share into two equal piles, and that is the whole trick to them. Every row below is split down the middle into two equal halves, because every even number is a double. Step 14 added the odd numbers up and landed on a square. Do the same with the evens and you land somewhere just as tidy, but not the same shape. How many even numbers: 4 Each row split into two equal halves 20 = 4 × 5 Where does an even number sit? Halve it. The evens against the odds Odd numbers make a square, even numbers make a rectangle. The first four odd numbers add to 16, a 4 by 4 square. The first four even numbers add to 20, a 4 by 5 rectangle: one row taller. The gap between the two totals is never a surprise. Every even number is exactly one more than the odd number just before it. There are n of them, so the evens total is always n more. And because every even number is a double, adding them up is really adding the counting numbers twice over. 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 is two lots of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. That is twice the triangle from Step 7. Step 16 The order of the operations 3 + 4 × 5 has two possible answers. Work along the line and you get 35; do the multiplication first and you get 23. Only one of those is what the expression means. The way it is settled will be familiar from Step 21: it is a convention . Everybody agreed on it so that everybody reads the same line the same way, and nobody discovered it. The agreement is that × and ÷ are done before + and − . An expression 23 is the answer What the agreement is worth Operations of the same rank are done left to right, and that matters more than it looks. 10 − 2 − 3 is 5 because you take 2 away and then 3. steps.t: A factor of a number divides into it exactly, with nothing left over. A multiple of a number is what you get by counting it up: the times table. They point in opposite directions, and the difference between them is the thing to hold on to. The factors of a number are a short list that stops. Its multiples go on for ever. Factors also come in pairs , and where the two halves of a pair meet turns out to be the square root from Step 4. Pick a number Its factors, joined up in pairs 8 factors And the other direction: its multiples All eight, side by side Factors stop. Multiples do not. Every number has a first factor (1) and a last one (itself), so the list is finite and you can write all of it down. Nothing is the last multiple, so you write the first few and then three dots. The pairs are why you never have to test very far. Sorting the factors of 24 into pairs gives 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6. After 4 the pairs would just repeat backwards, because 4 × 6 and 6 × 4 are the same pair. The turning point is the square root, which is exactly the stopping rule Step 4 gave you. And a square number is the only kind with an odd number of factors . One of its pairs is a number paired with itself. 36 gives 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and then 6 × 6, which is nine factors, not ten. The next step is about the numbers at the other extreme - the ones with exactly two.
steps.g: fraction geometry odd and even position sequence statistics subtraction

steps.t: Put two numbers side by side and ask what they have in common. A common factor divides into both of them; a common multiple is in both times tables. Watch the names carefully, because they are not the same shape. We talk about the highest common factor but the lowest common multiple. Step 17 already explained why. Factor lists stop, so there is a highest one to find. Multiple lists never stop, so there is no highest - only a first. Two numbers Their factors, and the overlap 6 highest common factor Multiples of Multiples of 36 lowest common multiple All six pairs Highest for factors, lowest for multiples - and the asymmetry is not a quirk of the words. Both factor lists stop, so the numbers in both stop too, and asking for the highest is a fair question with an answer. Neither multiple list stops, so their common ones go on for ever: 36, 72, 108, 144 and so on without end. There is nothing to call a highest common multiple, so the one worth naming is the first. Two shapes come up again and again. When one number divides the other, they have done the work for you. 8 and 16 share a highest factor of 8 and a lowest multiple of 16, the two numbers themselves. When they share nothing but 1, as 7 and 11 do, the lowest common multiple is simply the two multiplied together. And one thing is worth checking on every row of the table. The highest common factor times the lowest common multiple always comes to the two numbers multiplied. 6 × 36 = 216, and 12 × 18 = 216 as well. Step 19 Divisibility rules Step 17 asked what divides into a number, and answered it by trying every number in turn. For the small divisors you do not have to. Each one has a rule that reads only part of the number, sometimes a single digit. It tells you the answer without dividing at all. Pick a n

steps.t: By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Explain the values of repeated digits in a number, including decimals. Decompose numbers into their place value parts, including decimals. Multiply and divide whole numbers by 10, 100 and 1000. Position positive and negative numbers around zero. Round numbers with one decimal place to the nearest whole number.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Place value with decimals Place value carries on past the decimal point - the first digit after it is tenths, the next is hundredths, each worth ten times less than the one before. Part 2 of 3 Negative numbers and rounding Negative numbers sit to the left of zero on a number line. Rounding a decimal means finding which whole number, or which tenth, it is nearer to. Part 3 of 3 Fractions, percentages and ratio A fraction, a percentage and a ratio can all describe the same relationship between two amounts, just written in different ways.

Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them. Step 21 Rounding Rounding replaces a number with the nearest round one, so it can be said, remembered and compared without carrying every digit around. It is the same kind of move as Step 19: look at one particular digit and decide. The difference is which digit. A divisibility rule reads the digits at the end of the number. Rounding reads the single digit just after the place you are rounding to. Nothing else matters at all. A number To the nearest Which one is it nearer? 3,500 to the nearest 100 The same number, rounded four ways And the same rule on a number with a decimal Round in one move, from the number you started with. Rounding twice is the mistake worth guarding against, and 149 is the clearest case. To the nearest ten it is 150, and 150 to the nearest hundred is 200. But 149 to the nearest hundred is 100 , because its tens digit is 4. The first answer went through a number that was already not the original. The second reading of 5-or-more was made about a digit that rounding had put there. 3,449 does the same thing: 3,450 then 3,500, against a true answer of 3,400. Exactly halfway goes up, and that is a convention rather than a fact. 3,450 is the same distance from 3,400 as from 3,500, so nothing about the number decides it. Everybody agrees to go up, so everybody gets the same answer. And a rounded number is not the number. 27,849 people rounds to 28,000. That is a fair thing to print in a headline and the wrong thing to put on a ticket order. The whole point of rounding is that you have deliberately thrown some of the number away, so it is worth knowing how much. Here it is 151 people. Spot the mistake Your teacher says: 3.7 and 4.5 both round to 4 to the nearest whole number.

Counting down from 5 does not stop at 0. It carries straight on into −1, −2, −3. The number line runs just as far to the left of zero as it does to the right. The minus sign is not saying how big a number is - it is saying which side of zero it is on. That one idea settles everything else in this step. It settles the thing almost everybody gets wrong the first time: −7 is lower than −3, even though 7 is bigger than 3. Morning: 5 °C Night: −3 °C 8 degrees apart Which of each pair is the lower number? Written down, the sign always opens towards the bigger number, so −7 < −3 reads “minus seven is less than minus three”, and −10 = −10 says they are the same number twice. The minus sign says which side of zero, not how big. On the right of zero the numbers get bigger as you go along. On the left they get smaller , so the digits count downwards. −1, −2, −3 are each lower than the one before. That is the whole reason −7 sits below −3 while 7 sits above 3. Reading it off the line takes no thought at all. Whichever mark is further left is the lower number, every time, no matter what the digits say. Zero is neither. It is not positive and not negative. It is the one number that only marks the boundary. Every negative number is below it, and every positive one is above. So any negative beats any positive to the bottom, however small its digits look: −1 is colder than 40. Counting across zero is done in two parts. From 5 down to −3 you go 5 steps to reach zero and 3 more after it, which is 8. And 8 is exactly 5 + 3. That is why the distance between a positive and a negative is found by adding rather than subtracting. And this is not only about temperature. A submarine at −40 metres is fo

steps.t: A fraction cuts a whole into equal parts and then counts some of them. The number underneath says how many parts the whole was cut into ; the number on top says how many you have. Notice that the bottom number is not a size. It is a count of cuts, and that is where the trap lives, for the third time in a row. 1/4 has the bigger number underneath and is the smaller amount. Cutting a cake into four gives you smaller pieces than cutting it into three. A fraction The whole, cut up and counted 0.75 as a decimal The very same amount, written other ways Which of each pair is the bigger amount? Cutting into more pieces makes each piece smaller. That is the whole of the first trap: 1/4 < 1/3 although 4 > 3. The bottom number counts cuts rather than measuring an amount. And it is the third version of the same mistake in three steps. Below zero, bigger digits could mean a lower number; with decimals, more digits could mean a smaller one; here, a bigger number underneath means less. In every case a numeral was read as a size while it was doing some other job. It was naming a side of zero, filling a column, or counting cuts. Equivalent fractions cost nothing because you do the same thing twice. Multiplying top and bottom by 2 cuts every piece in half and then takes twice as many of them, so the amount cannot change. 3/4, 6/8, 9/12 and 75/100 are one amount with four names. Which is also how you compare two of them. Rewrite both with the same number underneath and then only the top numbers matter. 2/3 and 3/4 become 8/12 and 9/12, and the answer is immediate. A decimal is just a fraction that has agreed on its bottom number in advance. Step 23’s 0.65 is 65/100, which tidies up to 13/20. And it is worth knowing that not every fraction can be written as a decimal that stops. 1/3

steps.t: Per cent means for each hundred - the same cent as in century and centimetre - so 65% is simply 65 out of every 100. That makes a percentage a fraction whose bottom number was agreed in advance, which is exactly what Step 23 said about a decimal. All three steps have now described the same thing: 65%, 65/100 and 0.65 are one number wearing three costumes. The square below is the same picture Step 25 drew for 65/100 with a different name on it. A percentage A hundred squares, that many shaded 20 of 80 One number, three costumes The ones worth knowing without working them out Percentages exist to settle arguments about fractions. Is 17 out of 25 better than 33 out of 50? The second one has bigger numbers in it, which tells you nothing. And Step 25’s method, rewriting both over the same bottom number, needs you to pick a bottom number first. A percentage picks it in advance and always picks the same one. So every share in the world can be compared at a glance: 68% > 66% , and the argument is over. Finding one is two divisions and then some adding. 10% is the number divided by ten and 1% is the number divided by a hundred. Every percentage from 1 to 99 can be built out of those two. 65% of 80 is six tens (48) plus five ones (4), which is 52. If the fraction is a friendly one, go that way instead - 25% is 1/4, so 80 ÷ 4 = 20 in a single move. 100% is the whole thing, and there is nothing stopping you going past it. 150% is one and a half, which is why the square above draws a second hundred when you ask for it. It is also why a price that rises by 150% ends up two and a half times what it was, rather than one and a half.

steps.h: Part to part, part to whole
steps.t: Two ways of describing one mix of counters, and the whole difference is what each of them compares. A ratio compares part to part: three orange to two teal, written 3 : 2 . A proportion compares part to the whole: three of the five counters are orange, which is 3/5 , or 60%. Same picture, two true sentences, and the numbers in them are not the same numbers. The mix 60% are orange Every mix, read both ways The commonest mistake is reading a ratio as a fraction. 3 : 2 does not mean 3/2, and it does not mean three out of two, which is not a thing. Both of its numbers are parts , and the whole is what you get by adding them. 3 + 2 = 5, so the proportion is three out of five. The colon and the fraction bar look similar and mean quite different things. A ratio simplifies exactly like a fraction, though. 6 : 4 is the same mix as 3 : 2. Doubling both parts changes how many counters are on the table, not how they are shared. That is the same argument Step 25 made about 3/4 and 6/8. And a proportion is the one you can turn into a percentage , because a percentage compares part to whole too. A ratio cannot be a percentage on its own; you have to find the whole first.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Apply skills of rounding and calculating to problems. Decide whether to work mentally, with jottings or using a formal method. Estimate and multiply whole numbers by 1-digit or 2-digit numbers. Estimate and divide whole numbers by 1-digit numbers.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Choosing a method Some calculations are quick enough to do in your head, some need jottings, and some need a full written method - part of solving a problem is choosing which. Part 2 of 3 Estimating first Before working out an exact answer, a quick estimate tells you roughly what to expect, so you can tell if your exact answer is reasonable. Part 3 of 3 Reading the story A real-life problem hides its numbers inside a story - read it carefully, find what is being asked, then choose your method.

Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them. Step 28 Squares and sequences in real life A word problem never says "this is a sequence". So do it in two moves: first decide which tool the problem needs, then do the maths. Twenty-seven problems, one at a time. Move 1 · What kind of problem is this? A square, cube or triangle number Keep doing the rule Find the rule from the terms Count the pattern, then the rule Check what divides into it Round it to a useful place Turn it into a percentage Move 2 · Work it out Next problem 0 % Do them again Count the hops, not the terms. To get from the 1st term to the 8th you use the rule 7 times. Writing the sequence out is never wrong, but "start + 7 × step" gets there faster.

steps.t: The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Sorting by the sides Triangles are named by how many sides are the same length - all three, exactly two, or none. The angles always agree with the sides, so an equilateral triangle has three equal angles and a scalene triangle has none. Part 2 of 3 Naming an angle by eye A right angle is 90 degrees, the corner of a page. Smaller than that is acute and larger is obtuse, so you can classify an angle by holding a corner against it without measuring anything. Part 3 of 3 Round the edge, or inside Perimeter is the distance all the way round and area is how many squares fit inside. They answer different questions, which is why two rectangles can use the same length of fence and hold different amounts of room.

Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them. Step 29 Three kinds of triangle Triangles are sorted by how many of their sides are the same length. Pick a kind and look at what that does to the angles and to the lines of symmetry — the sides and the angles always agree with each other. Choose a kind of triangle What is true about it Equal sides and equal angles come as a pair. Where two sides are the same length, the two angles opposite them are equal too. That is why a scalene triangle, with no two sides the same, also has no two angles the same — and why it has no line of symmetry at all. Step 30 Acute, right or obtuse A right angle is exactly 90°, the corner of a page. Everything smaller is acute, everything larger (up to a straight line) is obtuse. Drag the arm and name the angle before you read the label. Open the angle Your turn: what kind is it? Estimate against the right angle. You do not need a protractor to classify one. Hold the corner of a page against it: if the arm falls inside the corner it is acute, if it falls outside it is obtuse.

Two angles that sit together on a straight line always add to 180°. That is enough to work out one you cannot measure, as long as you know the other. Move the arm Find the missing angle Subtract from 180, not from 90. The commonest slip is to reach for 90 because a right angle is the angle you know best. On a straight line the total is 180°, so the missing angle is 180 minus the one you have. Step 32 Perimeter is not area Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Area is how many squares fit inside. They measure different things, and changing a shape can move one while the other stays exactly where it was. Build a rectangle Every rectangle with perimeter 24 Same perimeter, different area. All of those rectangles use 24 cm of edge, and their areas run from 11 to 36 squares. So knowing the perimeter tells you nothing on its own about how much room is inside — the squarer the rectangle, the more area the same edge encloses.

A compound shape is not a shape with its own formula — it is rectangles stuck together. Cut it into rectangles you can already do, work each one out, then add. For the perimeter, walk all the way round the outside instead. Working The cut line is not part of the perimeter. When you split the shape, the new edge down the middle belongs to both rectangles — it helps you find the AREA, but it is inside the shape, so it is never walked when you measure the distance round the outside. Step 34 Solids and the nets that fold into them A solid keeps its faces, edges and vertices however you turn it — a cube lying on a corner is still a cube. A net is that solid opened flat, and not every arrangement of six squares folds back up. Choose a solid Which of these fold into a cube? Six squares is necessary, not sufficient. Every one of these has six squares. A net fails when two squares would land on the same face as it folds — so count the squares first, then check the arrangement.

A mirror line means every square has a partner the same distance away on the other side. Click the squares on the right to complete the reflection. Where the mirror is Count from the line, not from the edge. A square two columns from the mirror reflects to two columns from the mirror on the other side. Counting from the edge of the grid instead is what makes a pattern come out shifted.

lessons.title: Where Things Are and How They Move

steps.t: By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Compare the relative position of coordinates, with or without the aid of a grid. Use knowledge of 2D shapes and coordinates to plot points to form lines and shapes in the first quadrant. Translate 2D shapes, identifying the corresponding points between the original and the translated shape. Reflect 2D shapes in both horizontal and vertical mirror lines to create patterns on square grids.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Along first, then up A coordinate pair names one place only because the order is fixed - the first number is how far along and the second is how far up. Swap them and both numbers are still right while the point is somewhere else entirely. Part 2 of 3 A slide keeps the shape facing the same way Translating a shape moves every vertex by the same amount in the same direction. Nothing turns and nothing changes size, so if one corner goes three right and two up, all of them do. Part 3 of 3 A reflection turns it to face the mirror Reflecting flips the shape across a line. Each point lands the same distance on the other side, so a vertex close to the mirror stays close and a far one stays far.

Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them. Step 36 Along first, then up A coordinate pair says how far ALONG and then how far UP. The order is fixed, so (3, 1) and (1, 3) are two different places. Read the marked point and choose its pair. Which pair is the marked point? Try another point Along the corridor, then up the stairs. The commonest mistake is to give the pair the wrong way round. Both numbers are correct and the point is still wrong, which is why the order is worth a saying you can repeat. Step 37 Plot the shape Coordinates do more than name a spot — plot several and they give you the vertices of a shape. Click the four points in the list, then see what you have drawn. Plot these vertices A shape is its vertices. Four points are enough to fix a rectangle completely — no measuring is needed, because the coordinates already say how long each side is.

Maps and plans often mark only the numbers along the edges. The point is still exactly where the lines would have crossed, so you count from the axes instead of tracing a line. Where is the point? Line up with the edge. With no gridlines, put a ruler or a straight edge from the point down to the bottom axis to read the first number, then across to the side axis for the second. Step 39 Slide it, do not turn it A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. Nothing turns and nothing changes size, so every vertex moves by exactly the same amount. Choose a translation Where each vertex lands Every vertex moves the same way. If one corner goes 3 right and 2 up, they all do. That is the check: work out one vertex, then add the same pair to the others rather than re-reading the grid each time. Step 40 Describe the move Reading a translation is the same skill backwards. The faded shape is where it started and the solid one is where it finished — say what happened. Which translation was it? Pick one corner and follow it. You do not need the whole shape. Choose a single vertex you can find in both positions, and the change in its coordinates IS the translation.

A reflection flips a shape across a mirror line. Each point lands the same distance on the other side, so a point close to the line stays close and a far one stays far. Where is the mirror? Each vertex and its image A reflection is not a slide. A translation keeps the shape facing the same way; a reflection turns it round to face the mirror. A shape that looks unchanged after reflecting is one whose mirror line is its own line of symmetry.

lessons.title: Time and How We Write It

steps.t: By the end of this lesson you will be able to... Understand time intervals less than one second. Compare times between time zones in digital notation (12- and 24-hour) and on analogue clock faces. Find time intervals in seconds, minutes and hours that bridge through 60. Recognise that a time interval can be expressed as a decimal, or in mixed units.

The whole lesson, in three parts. Part 1 of 3 Sixty, not ten Time is the one measure that does not carry at ten or at a hundred. Minutes carry at sixty and hours at twenty-four, which is why an interval across the hour is worked in two hops rather than subtracted like ordinary numbers. Part 2 of 3 The same moment, written differently A 24-hour clock needs no am or pm because it never repeats itself; after midday you add twelve to the hour. The same length of time can also be written in mixed units or as a decimal, and 0.5 hours is thirty minutes rather than fifty. Part 3 of 3 Smaller than a second, and further than a country A race is timed to hundredths, so the gap between two runners is often a fraction of one second. At the other end of the scale, the same moment is a different clock time in another time zone, sometimes on another day.

Tap each word to see what it means and how to use it. Then show you know them. Step 42 Less than a second A second is not the smallest piece of time. Races are timed to hundredths, and the gap between two runners is often far less than one second. Line the two finishes up and read the difference. The finish times Line up the decimal points, then subtract. 10.4 and 10.35 look as though the second is bigger because it has more digits. Writing 10.4 as 10.40 puts both on the same footing, and the gap is five hundredths of a second. Step 43 The same time, written twice A 24-hour clock never repeats itself, so it needs no am or pm. After midday you add 12 to the hour, which is the whole rule. Move the clock and watch both ways of writing it. Move through the day Both clocks Write 16:45 the other way Midnight and midday are the two that catch people out. 00:30 is half past midnight, not half past midday, and 12:30 is half past midday. Everything between 13:00 and 23:59 is the afternoon or evening with 12 added.
steps.g: addition comparison fraction multiplication position time

steps.t: Minutes do not carry at ten or at a hundred — they carry at sixty. So an interval that crosses the hour is easier in two hops: up to the hour, then on from it. How long is that? Do not subtract the digits as if they were ordinary numbers. From 09:50 to 10:20 is not 70 minutes, and it is not 30 either if you take 50 from 20 and ignore the borrow. Ten minutes gets you to 10:00, then twenty more: thirty in total. Step 45 Half an hour, or 0.5 hours The same length of time can be written in mixed units, as a fraction of an hour, or as a decimal. They are three ways of saying one thing, and a timetable or a wage slip may use any of them. Choose a length of time Three ways to write it 0.5 hours is thirty minutes, not fifty. The decimal is a fraction of SIXTY minutes, so 0.5 means half of sixty and 0.25 means a quarter of it. Reading the digits after the point as minutes is the mistake this step exists to stop. Step 46 What time is it there? Clocks around the world are set to different hours, so the same moment is a different time in each place. Pick a city and compare it with Mogadishu. Compare Mogadishu with The time here The same moment A time zone can push you into another day. When the difference carries past midnight, the other city is on yesterday or tomorrow. The panel says so when it happens, because a time with no day attached can be read twelve or twenty-four hours wrong.
